title: Check if a given number exists in an array (linear search — loop through and compare each element).
shortTitle: Check if a given number exists in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Linear search walks the array from start to end comparing each element with the target. The moment a match is found it returns true (early exit); if the loop ends without a match it returns false. It runs in O(n) worst case and O(1) space, and it works on unsorted data, unlike binary search.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants to confirm whether a specific cheque of Rs.9800 was ever cleared on her account CUR3001. She reads cleared cheques one by one. The instant she sees Rs.9800 she says "yes, found it" and stops reading. If she reaches the end of the list without seeing it, she concludes it was never cleared.
s1_definition.oneliner: Scan the array and return true at the first match; return false only after checking every element.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Linear search walks the array from start to end comparing each element with the target. The moment a match is found it returns true (early exit); if the loop ends without a match it returns false. It runs in O(n) worst case and O(1) space, and it works on unsorted data, unlike binary search.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants to confirm whether a specific cheque of Rs.9800 was ever cleared on her account CUR3001. She reads cleared cheques one by one. The instant she sees Rs.9800 she says "yes, found it" and stops reading. If she reaches the end of the list without seeing it, she concludes it was never cleared.

**One line to remember:** Scan the array and return true at the first match; return false only after checking every element.

sections.s2_technical:
Linear search is the simplest search. You loop over each element and compare it with the target. The key efficiency feature is the early return: as soon as you find a match you stop, because you only need to know whether it exists, not how many times. If no element matches, you return false after the loop.

For money, comparison uses `compareTo` returning zero for value equality, so `target.compareTo(current) == 0` correctly matches `9800` and `9800.00`. For primitive `int` arrays you would use `==`.

The best case is O(1) when the target is the first element. The worst case is O(n) when the target is last or absent. Average case is O(n/2), which is still O(n). Space is O(1). Linear search is the right choice when the array is unsorted; if it were sorted you could use binary search for O(log n), but sorting first only pays off if you search many times.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Priya disputes a charge and National Bank of India needs to verify: "Was a Rs.9800 cheque ever cleared on CUR3001?" The system holds her cleared cheque amounts and must answer yes or no. This is exactly how linear search works — scan and return true on the first match.

Problem 2 — The dispute system only needs a yes or no, not a count, so we should stop at the first match to save work on long lists. This is exactly why linear search uses an early return instead of scanning the whole list.

The code has an `Account` holding amounts and a `ChequeVerifier` class with a `contains` method. The demo checks whether Rs.9800 exists.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: cleared cheques `[1500.00, 9800.00, 640.00]`, target `9800`.

Step 1 — Compare `1500.00` with `9800` by value: not equal, keep going.

Step 2 — Compare `9800.00` with `9800` by value: equal. Return true immediately, so `640.00` is never examined.

Step 3 — The method returns true, and the demo logs YES.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Cheque Rs.9800 cleared on CUR3001? YES
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: cleared = [1500.00, 9800.00, 640.00], target = 9800
    │
    ▼
  ChequeVerifier.contains()
    │ 1500.00 == 9800? no → continue
    │ 9800.00 == 9800? YES ───→ return true (early exit)
    │ 640.00  (never reached)
    ▼
  return true
    │
    ▼
  Log: "Cheque Rs.9800 cleared on CUR3001? YES"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether a value exists in an array is a linear search. I loop through the elements comparing each with the target, and the moment I find a match I return true and stop, which is the early exit that makes this efficient when the element is near the front. If the loop finishes without any match, I return false. The worst case is linear time when the target is at the end or absent, and the space is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used linear search in the dispute resolution flow. When Priya disputed a charge, the system needed to confirm whether a specific cheque amount had ever cleared on her account. The dispute flow only needs a yes or no answer, not a count, so I stop at the first match rather than scanning the entire history, which matters when an account has thousands of cleared cheques.

For money I compare BigDecimal values with the compareTo method and check for zero, so an amount stored as nine thousand eight hundred matches one stored as nine thousand eight hundred point zero zero, because they are the same value even though their scale differs. I also note that linear search is the correct choice here because the cheque history is unsorted. If the data were sorted I could use binary search for logarithmic time, but sorting first only pays off when I expect to search the same data many times.
